### CANDIDATE DETAIL
#### 1. monogenic diabetes  —  Tier 1 — Definitive / Highly Plausible  (fitness 0.785)
**Link type:** shared pathway (Reactome:R-HSA-210745)

**Proposed mechanism:** Heterozygous pathogenic variant in HNF1A (HP:0005110) —DISRUPTS→ HNF1A (HGNC:11621); HNF1A (HGNC:11621) —DISRUPTS→ Pancreatic beta-cell function and insulin secretion (GO:0005675); Pancreatic beta-cell function and insulin secretion (GO:0005675) —LEADS_TO→ Impaired glucose homeostasis (HP:0011454); Impaired glucose homeostasis (HP:0011454) —LEADS_TO→ Diabetes mellitus (HP:0000823). Pathogenic variants in HNF1A (HGNC:11621) lead to haploinsufficiency, disrupting normal pancreatic beta-cell function and insulin secretion. This disruption impairs glucose homeostasis, ultimately manifesting as diabetes mellitus in both MODY3 and other forms of monogenic diabetes.

**How to falsify it:** Identification of individuals with pathogenic variants in HNF1A that exhibit normal glucose tolerance and no signs of diabetes mellitus, or if the specific variants found in patients are common in the general population (e.g., gnomAD allele frequency > 1%). _(variant: HGMD-VAL:R177H)_

**Why it matters:** Understanding the shared role of HNF1A in these conditions highlights potential therapeutic targets for improving insulin secretion and glucose control in monogenic forms of diabetes. Genetic testing for HNF1A variants can aid in accurate diagnosis and family counseling.

#### 2. maturity-onset diabetes of the young type 6  —  Tier 3 — Moderate / Emerging  (fitness 0.442)
**Link type:** shared pathway (Reactome:R-HSA-210745)

**Proposed mechanism:** HNF1A (HGNC:4904) —DISRUPTS→ Pancreatic beta-cell development and function (GO:0030171); NEUROD1 (HGNC:7797) —DISRUPTS→ Pancreatic beta-cell development and function (GO:0030171); Pancreatic beta-cell development and function (GO:0030171) —LEADS_TO→ Insulin secretion defect (HP:0005972); Insulin secretion defect (HP:0005972) —LEADS_TO→ Hyperglycemia (HP:0003194). Loss-of-function mutations in HNF1A (MODY3) and NEUROD1 (MODY6) both disrupt the critical pathway of pancreatic beta-cell development and function, ultimately leading to an insulin secretion defect and hyperglycemia.

**How to falsify it:** Identification of pathogenic variants in HNF1A or NEUROD1 that lead to a gain-of-function or dominant-negative effect would falsify the proposed loss-of-function mechanism for both diseases. _(variant: Any common (AF > 0.01) pathogenic variant in HNF1A or NEUROD1 in gnomAD.)_

**Why it matters:** Understanding the shared downstream effects of genetic defects in HNF1A and NEUROD1 on pancreatic beta-cell function can inform therapeutic strategies for diabetes, potentially allowing for shared treatment approaches targeting insulin secretion or beta-cell preservation.

#### 3. maturity-onset diabetes of the young type 1  —  Tier 3 — Moderate / Emerging  (fitness 0.431)
**Link type:** shared pathway (Reactome:R-HSA-210745)

**Proposed mechanism:** HNF1A (HGNC:4774) —DISRUPTS→ Regulation of insulin secretion and glucose metabolism (GO:0005958); HNF4A (HGNC:4779) —DISRUPTS→ Regulation of insulin secretion and glucose metabolism (GO:0005958); Regulation of insulin secretion and glucose metabolism (GO:0005958) —LEADS_TO→ Diabetes mellitus (HP:0000820); Diabetes mellitus (HP:0000820) —LEADS_TO→ Hyperglycemia (HP:0003124). Mutations in HNF1A (MODY3) and HNF4A (MODY1) disrupt the shared pathway regulating insulin secretion and glucose metabolism in pancreatic beta-cells, ultimately leading to diabetes mellitus and hyperglycemia.

**How to falsify it:** Identification of pathogenic variants in HNF1A or HNF4A that do not segregate with the phenotype in affected families, or evidence that the affected individuals have mutations in other genes not related to pancreatic beta-cell function. _(variant: gnomad.broadinstitute.org/variant/2-170974853-C-T)_

**Why it matters:** Understanding the shared role of HNF1A and HNF4A in glucose homeostasis can inform therapeutic strategies targeting common downstream effectors or pathways for both MODY1 and MODY3, potentially leading to more effective personalized treatment approaches.

#### 4. maturity-onset diabetes of the young type 10  —  Tier 3 — Moderate / Emerging  (fitness 0.423)
**Link type:** shared pathway (Reactome:R-HSA-210745)

**Proposed mechanism:** HNF1A (HGNC:4876) —DISRUPTS→ pancreatic beta cell function (GO:0005624); INS (HGNC:6050) —DISRUPTS→ pancreatic beta cell function (GO:0005624); pancreatic beta cell function (GO:0005624) —LEADS_TO→ Impaired glucose homeostasis (HP:0003076); Impaired glucose homeostasis (HP:0003076) —LEADS_TO→ Diabetes mellitus (HP:0000831). Haploinsufficiency of HNF1A (MODY3) and loss-of-function mutations in INS (MODY10) both disrupt the normal function of pancreatic beta cells, leading to impaired glucose homeostasis and ultimately diabetes mellitus.

**How to falsify it:** Discovery of a pathogenic variant in either HNF1A or INS in individuals diagnosed with the other disease type would falsify this hypothesis. _(variant: rs75947411 (a common pathogenic variant in HNF1A))_

**Why it matters:** Understanding this mechanistic overlap could inform therapeutic strategies by targeting common pathways in beta-cell dysfunction, potentially leading to novel treatments for both forms of MODY.

#### 5. maturity-onset diabetes of the young type 4  —  Tier 3 — Moderate / Emerging  (fitness 0.422)
**Link type:** shared pathway (Reactome:R-HSA-210745)

**Proposed mechanism:** HNF1A (HGNC:4811) —DISRUPTS→ pancreatic beta cell function (GO:0005623); PDX1 (HGNC:9180) —DISRUPTS→ pancreatic beta cell function (GO:0005623); pancreatic beta cell function (GO:0005623) —LEADS_TO→ maturity-onset diabetes of the young type 3 (MONDO:0010894); pancreatic beta cell function (GO:0005623) —LEADS_TO→ maturity-onset diabetes of the young type 4 (MONDO:0011667). Loss-of-function mutations in HNF1A (MODY3) and PDX1 (MODY4) both converge to disrupt the critical pathway of pancreatic beta cell function, leading to distinct yet mechanistically related forms of diabetes.

**How to falsify it:** If genetic studies reveal that mutations in HNF1A and PDX1 do not functionally impact the same downstream cellular processes in pancreatic beta cells, or if distinct molecular mechanisms are identified that do not converge on impaired beta cell function, this hypothesis would be falsified. For instance, if HNF1A mutations primarily affected insulin processing while PDX1 mutations exclusively impacted beta cell proliferation, despite both leading to hyperglycemia. _(variant: The absence of common pathogenic variants in gnomAD for known disease-causing mutations in HNF1A and PDX1 supports their role in rare monogenic diabetes, but does not falsify the shared downstream pathway.)_

**Why it matters:** Understanding the shared downstream impact on pancreatic beta cell function, despite distinct genetic origins, can inform therapeutic strategies. Targeting common pathways in beta cell dysfunction could potentially benefit patients with either MODY3 or MODY4, or other forms of monogenic diabetes with similar underlying molecular defects.

#### 6. hyperproinsulinemia  —  Tier 3 — Moderate / Emerging  (fitness 0.418)
**Link type:** shared pathway (Reactome:R-HSA-210745)

**Proposed mechanism:** HNF1A (HGNC:4879) —DECREASES→ impaired insulin secretion (HP:0003237); impaired insulin secretion (HP:0003237) —LEADS_TO→ maturity-onset diabetes of the young type 3 (MONDO:0010894); INS (HGNC:6065) —DISRUPTS→ proinsulin processing and secretion (REACT:R-HSA-70326); proinsulin processing and secretion (REACT:R-HSA-70326) —LEADS_TO→ hyperproinsulinemia (MONDO:0014535); INS (HGNC:6065) —DISRUPTS→ proinsulin processing and secretion (REACT:R-HSA-70326). Mutations in HNF1A lead to impaired insulin secretion, causing MODY3. Mutations in the INS gene disrupt proinsulin processing and secretion, leading to hyperproinsulinemia. Both pathways converge on the regulation of insulin secretion and glucose homeostasis, with the INS gene product being central to the latter disease.

**How to falsify it:** Identification of pathogenic variants in HNF1A that do not lead to impaired insulin secretion or MODY3, or conversely, identification of pathogenic variants in INS that do not result in hyperproinsulinemia or related phenotypes. _(variant: rs104893737)_

**Why it matters:** Understanding the shared genetic and molecular basis of MODY3 and hyperproinsulinemia can inform the development of targeted therapies for both conditions, potentially improving glycemic control and reducing the risk of diabetes-related complications.

#### 7. Fanconi renotubular syndrome 4 with maturity-onset diabetes of the young  —  Tier 3 — Moderate / Emerging  (fitness 0.395)
**Link type:** shared pathway (Reactome:R-HSA-210745)

**Proposed mechanism:** HNF1A (HGNC:4804) —DISRUPTS→ Insulin secretion pathway; HNF4A (HGNC:4806) —DISRUPTS→ Insulin secretion pathway; HNF1A (HGNC:4804) —DISRUPTS→ Renal tubular reabsorption and glucose homeostasis; HNF4A (HGNC:4806) —DISRUPTS→ Renal tubular reabsorption and glucose homeostasis; Insulin secretion pathway —LEADS_TO→ Maturity-onset diabetes of the young (HP:0000775); Insulin secretion pathway —LEADS_TO→ Impaired glucose tolerance (HP:0011151); Renal tubular reabsorption and glucose homeostasis —LEADS_TO→ Fanconi renotubular syndrome (HP:0003413). Loss-of-function mutations in HNF1A and HNF4A disrupt both the insulin secretion pathway in pancreatic beta cells, leading to MODY, and the renal tubular reabsorption and glucose homeostasis pathways, contributing to Fanconi renotubular syndrome.

**How to falsify it:** The absence of mutations in HNF1A or HNF4A in individuals diagnosed with both MONDO:0010894 and MONDO:0014458, or the presence of pathogenic variants in entirely distinct genetic pathways for each disease, would falsify this hypothesis. _(variant: Presence of common benign variants in HNF1A or HNF4A (e.g., allele frequency > 1% in gnomAD) that do not segregate with either phenotype.)_

**Why it matters:** Understanding the shared molecular underpinnings of MODY and Fanconi renotubular syndrome, particularly the roles of HNF1A and HNF4A, could lead to novel therapeutic strategies targeting these transcription factors or their downstream pathways for both conditions. This could involve gene therapy, small molecule modulators, or metabolic interventions aimed at improving beta-cell function and renal tubular integrity.

**Why it matters:** Understanding the shared pathway of insulin regulation and secretion, despite originating from different genes and with different functional consequences, highlights the critical role of the insulin axis in both adult-onset and neonatal diabetes. This could inform targeted therapeutic strategies, such as personalized insulin replacement or incretin-based therapies, tailored to the specific genetic defect.
